hints: Remember what an ideal gas assumes, that particles have no volume and no attractions between them.
Low pressure keeps the argon atoms far apart, so their own volume and attractions become negligible.
High temperature gives the atoms high kinetic energy to overcome any attractions, so put the two most ideal conditions together.
walkthrough:
**Recall the ideal gas model**

An ideal gas is a perfect model where particles are point masses with no intermolecular forces.

Ideal gas equation:
$$pV = nRT$$

**See the effect of pressure**

At high pressure, particles are squeezed close together. Their actual volume matters and attractions increase, so deviation is large.

At low pressure, particles are far apart in a large volume, so they behave much more ideally.

**See the effect of temperature**

At low temperature, particles move slowly and intermolecular forces can hold them together, causing deviation.

At high temperature, particles have very high kinetic energy which overwhelms any attractions. So low pressure plus high temperature is most ideal.

options.A: High temperature is good for ideality, but high pressure is not. High pressure forces atoms close together so finite atomic volume and attractions become significant.
options.B: This is the least ideal combination. High pressure pushes particles together and low temperature allows attractions to dominate, so real gas deviation is greatest.
options.C: Low pressure keeps particles widely spaced and high temperature gives them energy to overcome attractions. Both factors make the assumptions of negligible volume and no forces most valid for argon.
options.D: Low pressure is good for ideality, but low temperature is not. At low temperature the kinetic energy is small, so even weak London forces between argon atoms cause deviation from ideal behaviour.
